justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 352.5 was anchored heavily on recent price action and short-term momentum, with very little deviation expected from the last observed level. The one-week estimate of 354.0 incorporated a slight continuation of that drift, consistent with a mild bullish bias in the near-term trend. The one-month estimate of 357.0 extended that logic further, assuming no major structural breaks and that the asset would continue grinding modestly higher in line with its recent trajectory. Across all three horizons, I was essentially assuming mean-continuation rather than mean-reversion, reflecting that no strong reversal signals were apparent at the time.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval of 344 to 361 is relatively tight because intraday and overnight price movements, while variable, tend to be bounded in the absence of major catalysts. By one week, the interval widens to 338–370, capturing the possibility of a few consecutive adverse or favorable sessions compounding into a more meaningful move. At one month, the interval of 326–389 is substantially wider, reflecting the many macro and idiosyncratic events that can unfold over four weeks. I also incorporated the general observation that implied or realized volatility at these horizons follows a square-root-of-time scaling roughly, though I widened the tails slightly beyond a purely mechanical calculation to account for jump risk.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro sentiment — such as an unexpected hawkish central bank decision, a geopolitical shock, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could drive prices well below 326 at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data release, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above 389. Liquidity conditions also matter; if market depth were to thin out around key technical levels, moves could overshoot my modeled ranges more readily than normal.

Finally, I want to be transparent that my intervals are probabilistic rather than guaranteed. A 90% confidence interval, by construction, is expected to be violated roughly one in ten times even if the model is perfectly calibrated. Model misspecification — particularly if the underlying volatility regime shifts or if there is a structural break in correlations — could mean my intervals are systematically too narrow. Forecasters routinely underestimate tail risk, and I have tried to lean slightly conservative on interval width, but readers should treat these ranges as informed estimates rather than hard bounds.
